questions.q: What is a JavaScript runtime, such as Node.js or a browser?
questions.explain: The JavaScript language has no way to read a file or open a connection. The runtime adds those: a browser gives you window and document; Node.js gives you files, servers and process.
options: A newer version of the JavaScript language
The program that runs your code and adds abilities the language lacks, like files or web pages
A tool that turns JavaScript into TypeScript
A library you install with npm to make code faster

questions.q: Which is true about the browser runtime compared with Node.js?
questions.explain: The browser protects your files for safety. Node.js is a runtime for servers and your own computer, so it can read and write files and start servers.
options: The browser can read any file on the computer; Node.js cannot
The browser has a web page but keeps you away from the computer's files; Node.js has no page but can use files and ports
Only the browser can run promises

questions.q: Run with Node.js. What does this print?
questions.explain: Node.js has no web page, so there is no window or document. Instead there is process, an object that describes the running program.
questions.code: console.log(typeof window, typeof document, typeof process);

questions.q: Run with Node.js. What does this print?
questions.explain: process.version is text like "v24.19.0". process.versions lists the version of each part, including the V8 engine, also as text.

questions.q: Which part of Node.js reads your JavaScript, turns it into machine code and runs it?
questions.explain: V8 is the JavaScript engine, written by Google for Chrome. That is why Chrome and Node.js print the same error messages.

questions.q: What does libuv do inside Node.js?
questions.explain: libuv is a C library. It waits for files, the network and timers, so your JavaScript does not have to, and queues the callbacks when the answers are ready.
options: It checks your code for syntax errors
It installs packages from the npm registry
It talks to the operating system (files, network, timers) and does the waiting for slow things

questions.q: How do the Node.js APIs such as node:fs fit in?
questions.explain: You import them with the node: prefix. They are built in, so nothing needs installing, and they use libuv underneath to reach the computer.
options: They replace V8 when reading files
They are JavaScript modules on top that pass your requests to libuv and give you back the results
They must be installed with npm install fs
They only work in the browser

questions.q: What does the event loop do?
questions.explain: When a file has been read or a timer is due, libuv puts the callback in a queue. The event loop runs queued callbacks one by one. When nothing is left to wait for, the program ends.
options: It runs every callback at the same time on many threads
It takes the next ready callback from a queue and runs it, over and over, until there is nothing left to wait for
It repeats your whole program in a loop
It checks for new npm versions

questions.q: Node.js runs your JavaScript on one thread. How can one server still answer thousands of people?
questions.explain: A backend mostly waits for databases and networks. That waiting does not use the JavaScript thread, which runs whichever callback is ready next.
options: It starts a new copy of Node.js for each person
Waiting is done outside your code (by libuv), so the thread is free to run other callbacks meanwhile
It answers only one person per second
Each request gets its own V8 engine

questions.q: This code runs inside a file-read callback, like most server code. What does it print?
questions.explain: Synchronous code first. Then the microtasks: nextTick, then promises. After the I/O callback, setImmediate runs, and the timer runs when the loop comes back round to its timers.

questions.q: The lesson's practice. What does this print?
questions.explain: Synchronous C first, then the microtasks (nextTick E, then the promise B), then setImmediate D after the I/O, and the timer A last.

questions.q: Run with Node.js. What does this print?
questions.explain: Sync code finishes first. process.nextTick callbacks run as soon as the current code finishes, even before promise callbacks, although the promise was scheduled earlier.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise callbacks are microtasks: they run as soon as the current code finishes, before the event loop moves on to timers, even a 0 ms timer.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: main runs until the await, then the rest of the file carries on (B). The code after await is a microtask, so it runs before the timer.

questions.q: Which two kinds of callbacks are called microtasks in the lesson?
questions.explain: Microtasks are small jobs that run right after the current code, before the event loop moves on to I/O, setImmediate and timers.
options: process.nextTick callbacks and promise callbacks (including code after an await)

questions.q: At the top level of a file, you schedule setTimeout(A, 0) and setImmediate(B). B must happen after A. What should you do?
questions.explain: Outside an I/O callback, which of the two runs first depends on how fast the program started. Never write code that depends on which timer wins.
options: Call B from inside A (or await A), because the order of the two is not fixed there
Use a larger delay for B, like 1 ms

questions.q: notify sometimes runs before the task is saved. Change handle() so it awaits save before calling notify, instead of relying on timer order. The program should print saved Buy milk and then notified.
questions.explain: If B must happen after A, await A (or call B from A). Guessing with timers is fragile: the order can change with load.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The timer was due after 10 ms, but the busy loop held the only thread for 50 ms. The timer could only run after the loop let go.
options:
busy loop finished
timer waited at least 50 ms

timer was on time
busy loop finished

busy loop finished
timer was on time

timer waited at least 50 ms
busy loop finished

questions.q: A route must process a huge file. What does the lesson recommend instead of one long synchronous job?
questions.explain: While long synchronous code runs, every timer and every other request waits. setTimeout(work, 0) only delays the blocking; it does not remove it.
options: Put the work in a while loop so it finishes faster
Do it in small pieces, with streams, or in a separate worker, so the loop is not blocked
Use setTimeout(work, 0) to run it all at once later

questions.q: How do you load Node.js's built-in file module in an ES module project?
questions.explain: Built-in modules use the node: prefix and need no install. require is CommonJS and does not exist in an ES module.
options: import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";, with nothing to install

questions.q: Which built-in module would you use for random ids and hashes?
questions.explain: node:crypto gives random ids, hashes and encryption. node:path builds file paths, node:os gives facts about the computer, node:events announces that something happened.

questions.q: Run with Node.js in an ES module project. What does this print?
questions.explain: fetch, URL and Buffer are global in Node.js. require belongs to CommonJS and does not exist in an ES module.
questions.code: console.log(typeof fetch, typeof URL, typeof Buffer, typeof require);

questions.q: You run node add.js add "Buy milk". Where do your own words start in process.argv?
questions.explain: process.argv is [pathToNode, pathToFile, "add", "Buy milk"]. Use process.argv.slice(2) to get only your arguments.
options: At index 2, after the path of node and the path of your file
At the end of the array

questions.q: What does process.argv.slice(2) hold after node args.js add "Buy milk"?
questions.explain: The terminal splits words on spaces, but quotes keep Buy milk together as one argument.

questions.q: Run with node args.js and no extra words. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first two items are always the paths of node and of your file. With no extra words, slice(2) gives an empty array.
questions.code:
const args = process.argv.slice(2);
console.log("arguments:", args, process.argv.length >= 2);

questions.q: Finish greet(argv). argv looks like process.argv: the name, if any, is at index 2. Return Hello, NAME!, or Hello, world! when there is no name. The program should print Hello, Ada! and then Hello, world!.
questions.explain: argv[2] is undefined when there is no argument, and ?? replaces undefined with the default. In a real program you pass process.argv.

questions.q: Finish parseCommand(argv): take the words after index 1, and return { command, title } where command is the first word and title is the rest joined with a space (or "" if there is none). The program should print { command: 'add', title: 'Buy milk' } and then { command: 'list', title: '' }.
questions.explain: argv.slice(2) drops the two paths. Destructuring with ...rest collects the remaining words, and join(" ") gives an empty string when there are none.

questions.q: What does an exit code of 0 mean?
questions.explain: Scripts, test runners and tools like Docker read the exit code to know whether your program worked. 0 is success; anything else is failure.
options: The program succeeded; any other number means failure

questions.q: What is the difference between process.exitCode = 1 and process.exit(1)?
questions.explain: Setting process.exitCode is gentler: the program ends normally with that code when there is nothing left to do. process.exit stops immediately.
options: exitCode only sets the code, so pending work (like a file being written) still finishes; exit(1) stops at once

questions.q: Why write a usage message with console.error instead of console.log?
questions.explain: Both appear in your terminal, but they are separate streams. You still set process.exitCode = 1 yourself to report failure.
options: It goes to the error output (stderr), so a script can tell errors apart from normal output (stdout)
It only shows up in the browser

questions.q: You run node learn-node/where.js from the folder above learn-node. What is process.cwd()?
questions.explain: process.cwd() is the working directory, not the file's folder; import.meta.dirname gives the file's folder. A relative path like "tasks.json" is looked up from the working directory.
options: The learn-node folder, where the file is
The folder above it, where your terminal was when you started the program
The folder where Node.js is installed

questions.q: Run with Node.js. What does this print?
questions.explain: process.memoryUsage() reports bytes as numbers. rss is all the memory the process holds; heapUsed is the part your JavaScript objects use, so it is smaller.
questions.code:
const { rss, heapUsed } = process.memoryUsage();
console.log(typeof rss, typeof process.pid, rss >= heapUsed);

questions.q: A server's heapUsed keeps growing for days and never goes down. What does that usually mean?
questions.explain: The garbage collector frees only objects nothing can reach. A cache or list that only ever grows keeps everything reachable, so memory climbs until the server fails.
options: The server is very busy, which is healthy
Something keeps objects it no longer needs: a memory leak
V8 is broken and must be updated

questions.q: Why should a database password come from an environment variable instead of being written in the code?
questions.explain: Settings that change between your computer and the server, and secrets above all, belong outside the code. Node.js puts environment variables in process.env.
options: Code is shared, copied and pushed to GitHub; secrets must never be, and the value differs per machine
Node.js cannot read strings from code files
It makes the program start faster

questions.q: Run with Node.js. What does this print?
questions.explain: Every value in process.env is a string (even the 5 became "5"), or undefined when it is not set. Convert and check it before you use it as a number.

questions.q: Run with Node.js, with QUIZ_PORT not set. What does this print?
questions.explain: The variable is undefined, so ?? uses the default 3000. A port is not a secret, so a default is fine.
questions.code:
const port = Number(process.env.QUIZ_PORT ?? 3000);
console.log(port, typeof port);

questions.q: The server needs TASKS_API_KEY. What should it do when the variable is not set?
questions.explain: A secret never gets a default. A server that starts without its key fails later in a confusing way, or runs without protection. Fail loudly at start-up.
options: Use a default like "dev-key" so it always starts
Start anyway and log a warning later
Refuse to start with a clear message, such as process.exit(1) after console.error
Generate a new key and print it to the log

questions.q: The config code wants to confirm the API key was loaded. What is the safe thing to print?
questions.explain: Secrets do not belong in logs. Logs are shared and stored, so the lesson prints only the key's length.
options: The whole key, so you can check it
The first half of the key
Only that it was loaded, for example its length
The key, but only in production

questions.q: You run PORT=5000 node --env-file=.env config.js, and .env has PORT=4000. Which port does the program see?
questions.explain: Values set before the command win. On a server, the hosting platform sets the real values this way, and the code only reads process.env.
options: 5000, because a variable already set in the terminal wins over the file
None: Node.js stops with an error

questions.q: On a server that sets real environment variables, there is no .env file. Which flag lets Node.js start anyway?
questions.explain: With --env-file=.env, a missing file stops Node.js before your code runs. --env-file-if-exists treats the file as optional.

questions.q: How should a project handle its .env file with Git?
questions.explain: .env holds real secrets and must never be committed. .env.example tells others which variables to set, without any real values.
options: Commit .env so other developers get the real secrets
Add .env to .gitignore, and commit a .env.example with the same names and empty or fake values
Commit .env, but in a private branch

questions.q: You pushed a real API key to GitHub by mistake. What must you do?
questions.explain: Once pushed, a secret stays in the Git history and may already be copied. Deleting the file does not help. Replace (rotate) the secret.
options: Delete the file in a new commit; that is enough
Make the repository private and keep the key
Treat the key as stolen: replace it with a new one, then remove it from the code
Nothing, if nobody has starred the repository

questions.q: Finish parsePort(env). env is like process.env. Use "3000" when PORT is missing. Return the number when it is a whole number from 1 to 65535; otherwise throw new Error(`PORT must be a whole number between 1 and 65535, got "${raw}"`). The program should print 3000, 8080, then the error message for abc.
questions.explain: Every value in process.env is text someone typed. Number("abc") is NaN, which is not an integer, so the check stops the program instead of starting on port NaN.
questions.expected:
3000
8080
PORT must be a whole number between 1 and 65535, got "abc"

questions.q: Finish loadConfig(env). If TASKS_API_KEY is missing or empty, throw new Error("TASKS_API_KEY is not set"). Otherwise return { port, apiKey }, with port from PORT as a number, defaulting to 3000. Never print the key itself. The program should print TASKS_API_KEY is not set, then Port: 4000, key has 12 characters.
questions.explain: The port gets a safe default; the secret never does. !apiKey catches both undefined and an empty string. Only the key's length is printed, never the key.
questions.expected:
TASKS_API_KEY is not set
Port: 4000, key has 12 characters

questions.q: Finish run(argv) for node add.js <title>. When there is a title at index 2, print Added: TITLE and return exit code 0. Otherwise print Usage: node add.js <title> and return 1. The program should print Added: Buy milk, exit code 0, Usage: node add.js <title>, exit code 1.
questions.explain: 0 means success and anything else means failure. In a real program you would write process.exitCode = run(process.argv); and print the usage with console.error.
questions.expected:
Added: Buy milk
exit code 0
Usage: node add.js <title>
exit code 1

questions.q: Finish toMb(bytes), which turns a byte count from process.memoryUsage() into megabytes with one decimal and " MB" after it (1 MB = 1024 × 1024 bytes). The program should print 51.0 MB and then 3.8 MB.
questions.explain: Divide by 1024 twice to go from bytes to megabytes, and toFixed(1) keeps one decimal, even when it is .0.

questions.q: Finish toExample(envText), which turns the text of a .env file into a safe .env.example: keep each variable name, but remove every value (keep the =). Skip empty lines. The program should print PORT= and TASKS_API_KEY= on two lines.
questions.explain: .env.example lists the names other developers must set, with no real values. You commit it; the real .env stays in .gitignore.
